intro: Devon reads his beach paragraph aloud and runs out of air halfway through, because the whole thing is one sentence. Across the hall, a book club argues about an old tale until three people are talking at once and nobody hears anybody. Both rooms have the same problem. The words are there. The shape that lets people follow them is not.

This unit is about that shape. First, the grammar of a sentence: subjects and predicates, the kinds of words that fill them, how to join sentences and how to fix ones that are broken or never stop. Then, the grammar of a conversation: how to prepare, listen, build on someone's idea, disagree without being rude, and give a short talk that a room can follow.

By the end you will be able to take a run-on apart and put it back together, make your verbs agree, pick their over there, and tell the difference between talking at people and talking with them. None of this is about sounding fancy. It is about being followed.
bigQuestion: How do the rules of sentences and the rules of talking help other people follow what you mean?

timeline.t: You split a sentence into its two halves: who or what, and what happens.
You sort the words in a sentence: nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions.
You join two short sentences with a comma and a conjunction, then with because or when.
You find the fragments and run-ons in a paragraph and fix each one a different way.
You make subjects and verbs agree, keep one tense, and choose their, there or they're.
You read a story, mark two spots, and bring one question to the circle.
You say back what the last speaker said before you add your own idea.
You plan a two-minute talk with an opening, three ordered points and an ending.
You record your talk, count the ums, fix one thing and record it again.
You give the talk to a real audience, at a pace they can follow, with one visual that helps.

words.d: the part of a sentence that tells who or what it is about
the part of a sentence that tells what the subject does or is
a joining word such as and, but, or, so
a sentence with a main part and a dependent part that cannot stand alone
a piece of a sentence that is missing a subject, a predicate or a main part
two or more full sentences jammed together without the right stop
to match in number: a singular subject with a singular verb, a plural with a plural
the verb form that tells when something happens: past, present or future
words that sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things
to connect your idea to what someone else just said
a short retelling of a speaker's main point and biggest reasons, in your own words
the people who are listening to you

test.q: In 'My cousin flew the kite,' what is the predicate?
test.why: The predicate tells what the subject did. The cousin flew the kite.
'They' stands in for a noun. Beach is a noun, ran a verb, slowly an adverb.

test.q: In 'The tiny crab hid under a rock,' which word is an adjective?
test.why: 'Tiny' describes the noun crab. Adjectives describe nouns.

choices: When the rain stopped, we went out.
The rain stopped, so we went out.
test.why: Two full sentences joined by a comma and the conjunction so make a compound sentence.

test.q: 'Because the bus was late.' How do you fix this fragment?
choices: Take out because and add a period
Add a main part, like 'we missed the bell'
test.why: A dependent clause needs a main part. 'Because the bus was late, we missed the bell' is complete.

choices: It rained, so we stayed in.
Because it rained, we stayed in.
test.why: Two full sentences with nothing between them is a run-on.

test.q: Which sentence has a verb that agrees with its subject?
test.why: Birds is plural, so the verb is sing with no -s.

test.q: What is the past tense of 'go'?
test.why: Go is irregular. Yesterday I went. Nobody says goed.

test.q: '___ going to leave ___ bags over ___.' Fill in order.
test.why: They're is short for they are, their shows owning, and there points to a place.

test.q: When is formal English the right choice?
test.why: Formal English fits school, work and people you do not know well.

test.q: What should you bring to a book discussion?
choices: One thing to say and one question to ask
Only your vote on the ending
test.why: Preparing means reading it all, marking spots and bringing one idea and one question.

test.q: Which shows you are building on someone's idea?
choices: I want to add to what Marcus said.
test.why: Building on means connecting your idea to what was just said, then adding.

test.q: A speaker says something confusing. What should a good listener do?
choices: Nod and hope it makes sense later
Ask a clarifying question, such as 'Can you give an example?'
test.why: Nodding is not understanding. A clear question helps you and everyone else in the room.

test.q: Why should a nervous speaker slow down?
choices: Slow feels strange to the speaker but sounds normal to listeners
Fast talking is against the rules
test.why: Nervous speakers race. What feels slow to you is what your audience can actually follow.

test.q: What is the best reason to record your own talk?
choices: To hear what your audience hears and fix one thing
test.why: A recording shows you what the audience hears. Fix one thing, then record again.

write.prompt: Devon's teacher said grammar is not a trap but a way to help people follow you. Do you agree? Make a claim, and back it up with evidence from Devon's run-on, the book club's second try, and at least one grammar rule from this unit.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: grammar and discussion rules do, or do not, help people follow you.
Use evidence: what happened when Devon added periods, and what changed when Sofia said back what Jamal meant.
Explain your reasoning: why does a period, a comma or a summary make a difference to the person listening or reading?
Give the other side: when are fragments or casual talk perfectly fine, and why?
Check your own writing for run-ons, fragments and agreement before you turn it in.

title: Grammar, Speaking and Listening

chapters.title: The Grammar of a Sentence
chapters.bigQuestion: What makes a group of words into a sentence that works?

story.title: The Sentence That Would Not Stop
story.kicker: Devon reads his own paragraph aloud, and about halfway through he runs out of air.
paragraphs: Mr. Alvarez asks Devon to read his paragraph to the class. Devon stands up. He takes a breath and starts. "On Saturday we went to the beach and it was hot and my cousin brought a kite and the wind was strong and the kite went up and then the string broke and we ran after it and a dog got there first." Devon's face turns red. He has not stopped once. He has not taken a breath.

The class laughs, but not in a mean way. A girl named Priya says, "That is one sentence? I got lost after the kite." Devon looks at his paper. She is right. It is one sentence. It is a sentence with eight little sentences stuffed inside it, all tied together with the word and.

Mr. Alvarez writes the whole thing on the board. Then he hands Devon a marker. "Find the places where you could stop," he says. Devon reads it again, slowly. He puts a period after hot. He puts one after kite. He puts one after broke. Now the paragraph has four sentences. He reads it again. This time he breathes.

"Nothing changed in the story," Mr. Alvarez says. "The beach is still hot. The dog still wins. But now a reader can follow you." He taps the board. "That is what grammar is for. Not to trap you. To help people follow you."

Devon sits down. He is still a little red. But he writes something at the top of his paper: Stop and breathe. This chapter is about the parts of a sentence and how they fit, so that every reader can follow you all the way to the dog.
story.think: Devon's story did not change when he added periods. So what did change, and why did it matter to the class?

lessons.title: Subject and Predicate
lessons.mainIdea: Every sentence has a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what happens), and it needs both.
reading: Look at this sentence: The dog got there first. Ask, who is this about? The dog. That part is the *subject*. Now ask, what did the dog do? Got there first. That part is the *predicate*. Every full sentence has both parts. Take one away and it falls apart.

The subject is the who or the what. It can be one word or several: Devon. My cousin's red kite. The strong wind at the beach. The predicate is the rest. It holds the action or tells what the subject is. Devon laughed. My cousin's red kite went up. The wind at the beach was strong.

Here is a quick test. Cover the subject with your hand. Does the rest still tell what happened? Cover the predicate. Does the rest still tell who? If either half is missing, you do not have a sentence yet. You have a piece of one.

words.d: the part of a sentence that tells who or what the sentence is about
the part of a sentence that tells what the subject does or is

look.title: Two Halves on the Board
look.text: Mr. Alvarez draws a line down the middle of the board. On the left he writes: The little brown dog. My cousin. The kite string. On the right he writes: broke with a snap. ran across the sand. barked at the waves. He asks the class to match a left side to a right side to make a sentence that makes sense.
look.prompt: Which left side goes with which right side? Could any left side match more than one right side?

check.q: In the sentence 'The wind was strong,' what is the subject?
check.why: The subject tells who or what the sentence is about. It is about the wind.

check.q: What does the predicate of a sentence do?
choices: Tells what the subject does or is
Ends the sentence with a mark
Names who the sentence is about
check.why: The predicate holds the action or tells what the subject is. 'Got there first' is a predicate.

check.q: 'My cousin's red kite' has no predicate. What is it?
check.why: It names a what, but nothing happens. Without a predicate, it is only a piece of a sentence.

lessons.title: Nouns and Pronouns
lessons.mainIdea: Nouns name people, places, things and ideas, and pronouns stand in for nouns so you do not repeat them.
reading: Read this: Priya lost Priya's pencil, so Priya asked Devon if Devon had seen Priya's pencil. Ouch. Now read this: Priya lost her pencil, so she asked Devon if he had seen it. Much better. The words her, she, he and it took the place of the names. Those words are *pronouns*.

First, the names. A *noun* is a word that names a person, a place, a thing or an idea. Priya, beach, kite and courage are all nouns. Some nouns name one thing: dog. Some name more than one: dogs. A noun that names one special person or place gets a capital letter: Devon, Chicago, Lake Michigan.

A pronoun stands in for a noun. I, you, he, she, it, we and they are the common ones. Here is the rule that matters: the reader must know which noun the pronoun replaces. Priya asked Devon, and he said no. Who said no? Devon, because he is the closest boy. If two boys were there, you would need the name again.

words.d: a word that names a person, a place, a thing or an idea
a word like she, it or they that stands in for a noun

look.title: Nouns in a Short Story
look.prompt: Which kind of noun shows up most in this story? Why might a story about a beach day be full of thing-nouns?

check.q: Which word is a noun?
check.why: A noun names a thing. 'Kite' names a thing. The others are a verb, an adverb and a pronoun.

check.q: Why do writers use pronouns?
choices: To repeat a name so no one forgets it
To stand in for a noun so it is not repeated
To show who is the most important
check.why: Pronouns like she and it take the place of nouns. That keeps the sentence from repeating a name over and over.

check.q: Which noun should have a capital letter?
check.why: Chicago names one special place. Nouns that name a special person or place get a capital.

lessons.title: Verbs, Adjectives and Adverbs
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs show action or being, adjectives describe nouns, and adverbs describe verbs.
reading: The kite went up. The kite is the noun. Went is the *verb*, the word that shows the action. Some verbs show a strong action: ran, snapped, barked. Some verbs show being, not doing: is, was, are. The sand was hot. Nothing moves, but was is still the verb.

Now add some color. The red kite went up. Red tells you more about the kite. A word that describes a noun is an *adjective*. The strong wind. A tiny dog. Three cousins. Adjectives answer which one, what kind, or how many.

One more. The kite went up fast. Fast tells you how it went up. A word that describes a verb is an *adverb*. Adverbs answer how, when or where. Many end in -ly: slowly, loudly, suddenly. The dog barked loudly. Loudly describes barked. Here is a trick: an adjective sticks to a noun, and an adverb sticks to a verb.

words.d: a word that shows an action (ran) or a state of being (is, was)
a word that describes a noun: red, tiny, three
a word that describes a verb and tells how, when or where: slowly, later, here

look.title: One Sentence, Built Up
look.text: The dog ran. The brown dog ran. The brown dog ran quickly. The small brown dog ran quickly across the wet sand and barked happily at the waves.
look.prompt: Which words are adjectives here? Which are adverbs? What does each one add that the first sentence did not have?

check.q: In 'The sand was hot,' which word is the verb?
check.why: 'Was' is a being verb. It does not show action, but it is still the verb.

check.q: What does an adjective describe?
check.why: Adjectives like red and tiny describe nouns. They tell which one, what kind or how many.

check.q: In 'The dog barked loudly,' what does 'loudly' tell you?
check.why: 'Loudly' is an adverb. It describes the verb barked and tells how.

lessons.title: Prepositions Show Where and When
lessons.mainIdea: A preposition is a small word like under, on or after that links a noun to the rest of the sentence.
reading: Where is the dog? The dog is under the table. On the table. Beside the table. Behind the table. Each little word tells you where the dog is. Those little words are *prepositions*. They link a noun (the table) to the rest of the sentence.

Prepositions can tell where: in, on, under, over, beside, between, across. They can tell when: before, after, during, until. They can tell other things too: with, for, about, of. A preposition never stands alone. It always comes with a noun or pronoun after it: after lunch, with my cousin, about the kite.

The preposition plus its noun is called a *phrase*. A phrase is a group of words that works together but is not a whole sentence. The string broke over the water. Over the water tells where. Take the phrase away and you still have a sentence: The string broke. Add it back and the reader can see the place.

words.d: a small word like under, on, after or with that links a noun to the rest of the sentence
a group of words that works together but is not a whole sentence

look.title: Move the Dog
look.text: Picture a small dog and a big red chair. Now say where the dog is, using one new little word each time. The dog is on the chair. The dog is under the chair. The dog is behind the chair. The dog is beside the chair. The dog jumps over the chair. Each time, the dog moves, and only one word changed.
look.prompt: Which word changed each time? What would happen to the picture if you took that word out and just said 'The dog is the chair'?

check.q: Which word is a preposition?
check.why: 'Under' links a noun to the rest of the sentence and tells where. It is a preposition.

check.q: What always comes after a preposition?
check.why: A preposition never stands alone. It needs a noun or pronoun: under the table, with him.

check.q: In 'We ate lunch after the race,' what does 'after the race' tell you?
check.why: 'After' is a preposition that tells when. The phrase 'after the race' tells the time of lunch.

lessons.title: Simple and Compound
lessons.mainIdea: A simple sentence has one subject and one predicate; a compound sentence joins two with a comma and a joining word.
reading: The wind blew. That is a *simple sentence*. One subject, one predicate, one complete thought. The kite went up. That is another. Two short sentences in a row can sound choppy. So writers join them: The wind blew, and the kite went up. Now it is one *compound sentence*.

Look at what holds the two halves together: a comma and the word and. The words and, but, or and so are joining words, also called *conjunctions*. Each one means something different. And adds. But shows a change. Or gives a choice. So shows a result. The string broke, so the kite flew away.

Here is the rule for the comma. When you join two full sentences with a conjunction, put a comma before the conjunction. The dog got there first, but Devon did not care. Both halves could stand alone, so the comma goes in. If the second half cannot stand alone, no comma: Devon laughed and sat down.

words.d: a sentence with one subject and one predicate that gives one complete thought
two simple sentences joined with a comma and a conjunction like and, but, or so
a joining word such as and, but, or, so

look.title: Same Story, Two Ways
rows: Version B: some joined into compounds
Version C: everything joined with and
look.prompt: Version C is Devon's one-breath paragraph. Version A is choppy. Why might Version B be the easiest to read?

check.q: Which one is a compound sentence?
choices: The wind blew, and the kite went up.
check.why: Two full sentences joined by a comma and 'and' make a compound sentence.

check.q: Which conjunction shows a result?
check.why: 'So' shows that one thing caused another: The string broke, so the kite flew away.

check.q: Where does the comma go in a compound sentence?
check.why: The comma goes right before the joining word: 'The dog got there first, but Devon did not care.'

lessons.title: Complex Sentences
lessons.mainIdea: A complex sentence joins a full sentence to a part that cannot stand alone, using words like because, when or although.
reading: Read this: When the string broke. Something is missing. You want to ask, what happened then? Now read: When the string broke, the kite flew away. There it is. The first part cannot stand alone. It leans on the second part. Together they make a *complex sentence*.

The part that cannot stand alone is a *dependent clause*. It depends on the rest. It starts with a word like because, when, if, although, after, before or since. The part that can stand alone is the main part: the kite flew away. A complex sentence has one of each.

The order can go either way. When the string broke, the kite flew away. Or: The kite flew away when the string broke. Notice the comma. If the dependent part comes first, put a comma after it. If it comes second, you usually need no comma. Complex sentences let you show why, when and what if.

words.d: a sentence with one main part and one dependent part that cannot stand alone
a part of a sentence that starts with a word like because or when and cannot stand alone

look.title: A Famous Sentence From Illinois
look.text: Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth on this continent, a new nation, conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln of Illinois, the Gettysburg Address, 1863
look.prompt: This is one long sentence. Find the subject and the main verb. Then find at least one phrase that tells when or where.

check.q: Which is a dependent clause?
check.why: 'Because the wind was strong' starts with because and cannot stand alone. It needs a main part.

check.q: When does a complex sentence need a comma?
choices: When the dependent part comes first
check.why: 'When the string broke, the kite flew away' needs the comma. 'The kite flew away when the string broke' does not.

check.q: What can a complex sentence show that a simple one cannot?
check.why: Words like because and when connect two ideas and show why, when or what if.

lessons.title: Fragments Are Missing a Part
lessons.mainIdea: A fragment is a piece of a sentence that is missing a subject or a predicate, and you fix it by adding the missing part.
reading: Read this: Ran after the kite. Who ran? You cannot tell. Now this: The kite over the water. What did the kite do? Nothing happens. Each of these is a *fragment*. A fragment looks like a sentence. It starts with a capital and ends with a period. But a part is missing.

There are two ways a fragment usually breaks. Either the subject is gone: Ran after the kite. Or the predicate is gone: The kite over the water. Sometimes a dependent clause is left alone: Because the dog was faster. That is a fragment too. It still needs a main part.

The fix is simple. Ask what is missing and add it. Ran after the kite becomes We ran after the kite. The kite over the water becomes The kite hung over the water. Because the dog was faster becomes Because the dog was faster, it won. Read your sentence aloud. If it leaves you waiting, it is a fragment.

words.d: a piece of a sentence that is missing a subject, a predicate or a main part
an idea that is finished on its own, with nothing left hanging

look.title: The Note on the Fridge
look.text: A note on the fridge says: Went to the store. Back at five. Milk in the bag. Nobody in the house is confused. They know Mom wrote it, and they know what she means. But every line is a fragment. Now imagine the same lines in a school report about a trip to a store.
look.prompt: Why are fragments fine on a fridge note but not in a report? What would you add to each line to make it a full sentence?

check.q: Which one is a fragment?
check.why: 'Ran after the kite' has no subject. Nobody is named as running. It is a fragment.

check.q: How do you fix a fragment?
check.why: A fragment is missing a subject, a predicate or a main part. Add the missing part and it becomes a sentence.

check.q: 'Because the dog was faster.' What is wrong?
choices: It is a dependent part with no main part
check.why: The clause starts with because and cannot stand alone. It needs a main part such as 'it won.'

lessons.title: Run-ons Never Stop
lessons.mainIdea: A run-on jams two or more sentences together without the right stop, and you fix it with a period, a comma and a conjunction, or a joining word like because.
reading: Devon's beach paragraph was a *run-on*. It had nine sentences tied together with and. A run-on is two or more full sentences that run into each other without the right stop. Here is a short one: The string broke the kite flew away. Two full sentences, no stop at all.

Some run-ons have a comma where a period should be. It was hot, we swam. That is called a comma splice, and it is still a run-on. A comma alone is too weak to hold two full sentences apart. It needs help.

You have three good fixes. One: use a period. The string broke. The kite flew away. Two: use a comma plus a conjunction. The string broke, so the kite flew away. Three: use a word like because or when. When the string broke, the kite flew away. Pick the fix that fits what you mean. Any of them lets the reader breathe.

words.d: two or more full sentences jammed together without the right stop between them
a run-on where only a comma sits between two full sentences

look.title: Words Between the Breaths
look.prompt: A reader usually breathes at a period. How many words did Devon's class have to hold in their heads at once before the fix? After?

check.q: Which one is a run-on?
choices: The string broke, so the kite flew away.
When the string broke, the kite flew away.
The string broke the kite flew away.
check.why: Two full sentences with nothing between them is a run-on. The others each have a proper stop or joining.

check.q: What is a comma splice?
choices: Two full sentences with only a comma between them
A missing comma in a list
check.why: A comma alone cannot hold two full sentences apart. 'It was hot, we swam' is a comma splice.

check.q: Which is NOT a good fix for a run-on?
choices: Use a comma and a conjunction
check.why: Stringing more sentences together with and makes the run-on worse. Devon's paragraph proved it.

lessons.title: Subject and Verb Agree
lessons.mainIdea: A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject takes a plural verb, and they must match.
reading: The dog barks. The dogs bark. Say them out loud. When the subject is one dog, the verb is barks. When there are two or more dogs, the verb is bark. The subject and the verb *agree*. They match in number. One dog, barks. Many dogs, bark.

It feels backward, and that trips people up. Adding -s to a noun makes it plural: dogs. Adding -s to a verb makes it singular: barks. So a plural subject usually takes a verb with no -s. The kids run. The kid runs. The waves crash. The wave crashes.

The tricky ones are is and are, was and were, has and have. She is here. They are here. He was late. We were late. It has a tail. They have tails. Watch out for words in between: The box of kites is heavy. The subject is box, not kites. Box is one thing, so the verb is is.

words.d: to match in number: a singular subject with a singular verb, a plural subject with a plural verb
one of something
more than one of something

look.title: Spot the Mismatch
look.text: My cousins likes the beach. The wind push the kite up high. A bag of shells sit by the towel. The dog and the boy runs to the water.
look.prompt: Each sentence has a subject and verb that do not agree. Find the subject in each, decide if it is one or more than one, and fix the verb.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Dogs is plural, so the verb is bark with no -s.

check.q: In 'The box of kites is heavy,' why is the verb 'is' and not 'are'?
choices: The subject is box, which is one thing
check.why: The subject is box. 'Of kites' is only a phrase in between. One box is heavy.

check.q: Which pair matches?
check.why: He is singular, and was is the singular past form. The others mix singular and plural.

lessons.title: Past, Present, Future
lessons.mainIdea: A verb's tense tells when something happens, and a piece of writing should stay in one tense unless the time really changes.
reading: The kite flies. The kite flew. The kite will fly. Same kite, same action, three different times. The form of the verb tells you when. That is called *tense*. Present tense is now: flies. Past tense is before now: flew. Future tense is later: will fly.

Most verbs make the past by adding -ed: jump, jumped. walk, walked. But many common verbs change in other ways. These are *irregular verbs*, and you learn them by ear and by heart. Go, went. Run, ran. See, saw. Eat, ate. Break, broke. Nobody says goed or breaked.

Here is the rule that matters most in writing. Pick a tense and stay in it. Read this: We went to the beach and my cousin brings a kite. Went is past, brings is present. The reader stumbles. Fix it: We went to the beach and my cousin brought a kite. Change tense only when the time really changes.

words.d: the form of a verb that tells when something happens: past, present or future
a verb that does not make its past tense with -ed, like go and went

look.title: Regular or Not?
rows: Verbs that add -ed (laughed, snapped, barked, wanted)
Verbs that change another way (went, ran, broke, got, was)
Verbs that stay the same (put, hit)
look.prompt: Nearly half of these verbs do not add -ed. Why does a writer need to know the irregular ones by heart?

check.q: Which verb is in the future tense?
check.why: 'Will' plus a verb shows a time that has not come yet.

check.q: What is the past tense of 'break'?
check.why: Break is irregular. Its past tense is broke, not breaked.

check.q: 'We went to the beach and my cousin brings a kite.' What is wrong?
choices: The tense changes for no reason
check.why: Went is past and brings is present. The time did not change, so the verb should be brought.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Word
lessons.mainIdea: Words that sound the same are spelled differently for a reason, and the words you choose should fit where you are and who is listening.
reading: Read this: There going to they're house over their. Every word is said right, and every one is spelled wrong. Their, there and they're sound the same. They are *homophones*. Their shows owning: their house. There points to a place: over there. They're is short for they are: they're going. Fixed: They're going to their house over there.

Other pairs trip people up too. Your and you're. Its and it's. To, too and two. The test is the same each time. Say the long form. If it's can become it is, use the apostrophe. If not, use its. The dog wagged its tail. It's a good dog.

Word choice also depends on where you are. With friends you might say, Yo, that kite was sick. In a class talk or a letter to the principal, you use *formal English*: That kite flew very well. Formal English uses full sentences, no slang, and no text-speak. Neither way is bad. A good writer knows which one fits the room.

words.d: words that sound the same but are spelled differently and mean different things
careful, full-sentence English for school, work and people you do not know well

look.title: Two Messages, One Kite
look.text: Devon sends his friend a text: kite broke lol dog got it first. Then he writes a note to the lifeguard who helped him find it: Thank you for helping me find my kite. The dog reached it before I did, but you got it back. Both messages tell the truth. Both say the same thing. They do not sound the same.
look.prompt: Why did Devon write the two messages so differently? What would happen if he swapped them?

check.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
check.why: 'They're' is short for 'they are.' They are going to the beach.

check.q: 'The dog wagged ___ tail.' Which fits?
check.why: The tail belongs to the dog. 'Its' shows owning. 'It's' would mean 'it is.'

check.q: When should you use formal English?
choices: In every text to a friend
In a class talk or a letter to the principal
check.why: Formal English fits school, work and people you do not know well. With friends, casual talk is fine.

review.q: What two parts does every full sentence need?
review.why: The subject tells who or what. The predicate tells what happens. A sentence needs both.

review.q: In 'The tiny dog barked loudly,' which word is an adverb?
review.why: 'Loudly' describes the verb barked and tells how. That makes it an adverb.

review.q: Which word is a preposition in 'The kite hung over the water'?
review.why: 'Over' links the noun water to the rest of the sentence and tells where.

choices: It was hot so we swam.
It was hot, so we swam.
It was hot so, we swam.
review.why: Two full sentences joined by a conjunction take a comma before the conjunction.

review.q: 'After the rain stopped.' What kind of problem is this?
review.why: It is a dependent clause with no main part. It leaves the reader waiting, so it is a fragment.

review.q: Which is the best fix for 'The bell rang the kids ran out'?
choices: The bell rang and the kids ran out and it was loud
The bell rang, the kids ran out.
When the bell rang, the kids ran out.
The bell rang the kids, ran out.
review.why: A word like when joins the two ideas properly. A comma alone makes a comma splice, and more ands make a longer run-on.

review.q: Which sentence has a subject and verb that agree?
choices: The kids runs to the water.
The kids run to the water.
The kid run to the water.
The kids is running to the water.
review.why: Kids is plural, so the verb is run with no -s.
'Their' shows owning. The kite belongs to them. The other sentences need there or they're.

chapters.title: Conversations and Presentations
chapters.bigQuestion: How do you talk so that people understand you, and listen so that you understand them?

story.title: Was the Ending Fair?
story.kicker: A book club of five fourth graders takes on an old tale, and the argument gets loud before it gets good.
paragraphs: Ms. Nakamura's book club sits in a circle on the rug. This week they read a very old story by Hans Christian Andersen, first printed in 1837, about a little mermaid. In the tale, the mermaid trades her voice to a sea witch for a pair of human legs. She hopes the prince will love her. He marries someone else. She is given a chance to save herself by harming him, and she refuses. At dawn she turns into foam on the sea.

Jamal starts. "That ending was not fair. She gave up everything and got nothing." Sofia jumps in before he finishes. "No, it was fair, she chose it!" Then three people talk at once. Nobody can hear anybody. Ms. Nakamura holds up one hand and waits. The circle goes quiet.

"Let's try that again," she says. "One person at a time. And before you answer, say back what the last person said." Jamal goes first, slowly. Sofia says, "Jamal thinks the ending was unfair because she gave up so much. I see that. But I think choosing not to hurt the prince was her own choice, and that makes it hers." Jamal nods. "Okay. But could you read me the part where she chooses? I want to hear it again."

Sofia finds the page and reads it aloud. Marcus, who has not spoken yet, says, "What if the story is not about whether she wins? What if it is about what kind of person she is?" The circle gets quiet in a different way. Everyone is thinking.

By the end, nobody has changed their vote. Jamal still says unfair. Sofia still says fair. But each one can explain the other side now. Ms. Nakamura writes on the board: Listen. Say it back. Ask. Build. This chapter is about how to talk and listen so that a conversation gets better instead of just louder.
story.think: The book club did not agree at the end. So how do you know the second try was better than the first?

lessons.title: Come Prepared
lessons.mainIdea: A good discussion starts before it starts: read the text, mark what you noticed, and bring one thing to say.
reading: Sofia came to book club with a sticky note on page 30. It marked the moment the mermaid throws the knife into the sea. When Jamal asked to hear that part, she found it in five seconds. That is what it looks like to *prepare*. She did the work before the circle formed.

Preparing for a discussion means three things. Read the whole text, not just the first pages. Mark places that surprised you, confused you or made you feel something. Then write down one thing you want to say and one question you want to ask. That is enough. You do not need a speech.

Being prepared changes how you feel in the circle. You are not scrambling. You are not hoping nobody calls on you. You have something to give. And when someone says, Where does it say that?, you can put your finger on the page.

words.d: to get ready ahead of time by reading, marking and planning what to say
a talk where a group shares ideas about one topic and listens to each other

look.title: Two Sticky Notes
look.text: Before book club, Marcus put two sticky notes in his book. One says: Page 12, she cannot talk anymore. Why did she agree to that? The other says: Page 30, I did not expect her to throw the knife. When the circle starts, he has a question and a surprise ready. Jamal has no notes and is flipping pages looking for the part he means.
look.prompt: Who is more likely to help the discussion move forward, and why? What would one sticky note have done for Jamal?

check.q: What does it mean to prepare for a discussion?
choices: Read, mark and plan one thing to say
Wait to hear what others think
check.why: Preparing means reading the whole text, marking spots and bringing one idea and one question.

check.q: Why did Sofia find the knife scene so fast?
choices: She had marked it with a sticky note
Ms. Nakamura told her the page
It was on the first page
check.why: She marked page 30 before club. Preparing means you can find the spot when someone asks.

check.q: What is a good thing to mark while reading?
choices: A part that surprised or confused you
check.why: Surprises, confusions and feelings make the best discussion spots.

lessons.title: Listen and Build On
lessons.mainIdea: Listening means taking in what someone said and connecting your idea to theirs, not just waiting for your turn.
reading: In the first try, Sofia talked before Jamal finished. In the second try, she said, Jamal thinks the ending was unfair because she gave up so much. Then she added her own idea. That is called *building on* what someone said. Her idea sat on top of his instead of knocking it over.

Real listening is not silent waiting. It is taking in the other person's words so well that you could say them back. Try these starters: I agree with Jamal because. I want to add to what Sofia said. That connects to what Marcus asked. Each one shows you heard, and each one moves the talk forward.

One more rule: eyes on the speaker, not on your own page. When you look at the person talking, you catch more than words. You catch when they are unsure. You catch when they are excited. A discussion works when people are listening to each other, not performing at each other.

words.d: to connect your idea to what someone else just said
to take in what someone says so well that you could say it back

look.title: Who Spoke in Ten Minutes
look.prompt: Two people took most of the turns. What could Jamal and Sofia do differently? What could the group say to bring in Elena?

check.q: What does it mean to build on someone's idea?
choices: Say something louder than they did
Change the subject to your idea
Connect your idea to what they just said
Repeat their idea word for word
check.why: Building on means your idea sits on top of theirs. You connect, then add.

check.q: Which sentence starter shows you were listening?
choices: I want to add to what Sofia said
I was not listening, can you repeat that
That is wrong, listen to me
check.why: 'I want to add to what Sofia said' shows you heard her and are connecting to her idea.

check.q: Why should your eyes stay on the speaker?
choices: So you look polite in the photo
So the teacher gives you a point
So you can plan what to say next
So you catch more than just the words
check.why: Watching the speaker helps you notice if they are unsure or excited, not only what they say.

lessons.title: Ask and Disagree Politely
lessons.mainIdea: Questions and polite disagreement make a discussion stronger, as long as you talk about the idea and not the person.
reading: Jamal did not give up his view. He asked Sofia to read the page again. That is a good question: it asks for *evidence*, the proof in the text. Other good questions are: What do you mean by that? Where does it say so? Why do you think that? A question is not an attack. It is an invitation.

Disagreeing is allowed. Being rude is not. Compare these. You are wrong and that is dumb. Or: I see it differently, because the story says she chose to throw the knife. The second one disagrees with the idea and gives a reason. It does not call anyone a name. That is *polite disagreement*.

Here is a pattern you can use every time. Say what you heard. Say you see it differently. Give your reason from the text. Sofia did all three in one breath, and Jamal nodded. Nobody lost. A discussion where everyone agrees in one minute is usually a discussion where nobody thought very hard.

words.d: proof, such as words from the text, that supports an idea
saying you see it differently and giving a reason, without attacking the person

look.title: The Wind and the Sun
look.text: In an old fable, the North Wind and the Sun argue about who is stronger. They pick a traveler in a coat. The Wind blows as hard as it can, and the man only pulls his coat tighter. Then the Sun shines gently. The man grows warm and takes the coat off by himself. The Sun wins without force.
look.cite: Aesop's fables, an ancient Greek tale, retold in our words
look.prompt: How is the Wind like a rude argument? How is the Sun like a polite one? Which one changed the traveler's mind?

check.q: Which is a polite way to disagree?
choices: That is dumb and you are wrong.
I see it differently, because the story says she chose.
check.why: It disagrees with the idea, gives a reason from the text, and does not attack the person.

check.q: What is evidence in a book discussion?
choices: Proof from the text, such as words on a page
check.why: Evidence is proof. In a book discussion, it is what the text actually says.

check.q: What does the fable of the Wind and the Sun suggest about arguments?
choices: Force changes minds better than warmth
Gentle reasons work better than blasting someone
check.why: The Wind blew hard and lost. The Sun was gentle and the man took his coat off himself.

lessons.title: Summarize What You Heard
lessons.mainIdea: A summary of a speaker gives the main point and the biggest reasons in your own words, in a few sentences.
reading: Jamal talked for a full minute about the ending. Then Sofia said, in one sentence, what he meant: Jamal thinks the ending was unfair because she gave up so much. That sentence is a *summary*. It is short. It is in Sofia's words. And it keeps the main point and the biggest reason.

To summarize a speaker, listen for two things. First, the main point: what does this person want me to believe or know? Second, the reasons: what did they say to back it up? Leave out the small stuff, the jokes and the side trails. Keep the point and the reasons.

A summary should be much shorter than the talk. If someone speaks for a minute, your summary might be two sentences. Say it back to the speaker if you can: So you are saying that. If they nod, you got it. If they say no, not quite, you just learned something before you argued about the wrong thing.

words.d: a short retelling of the main point and biggest reasons, in your own words
the one thing a speaker most wants you to know or believe

look.title: A Minute From Jamal
look.text: Okay so the mermaid, she gives up her voice, right, and that is like her best thing, and she gets legs but every step hurts, and then the prince does not even pick her, he picks the other girl, and she could have saved herself and she does not, and then she is just foam. So how is that fair? She did everything and got nothing.
look.prompt: Find Jamal's main point. Find his two strongest reasons. Now say the whole thing in two sentences.

check.q: What should a summary of a speaker keep?
choices: The main point and the biggest reasons
check.why: A summary keeps the point and the reasons and drops the small stuff.

check.q: About how long should a summary of a one-minute talk be?
check.why: A summary is much shorter than the talk. Two sentences is about right for one minute.

check.q: Why say your summary back to the speaker?
choices: To show you talk better than they do
To check that you understood before you respond
check.why: If they nod, you got it. If not, you learn that before you argue about the wrong thing.

lessons.title: Check What You Heard
lessons.mainIdea: When you are not sure what a speaker meant, ask a clear question instead of guessing.
reading: Marcus asked, What if the story is about what kind of person she is? Priya was not sure what he meant. She could have nodded and stayed lost. Instead she said, Do you mean the ending shows she is kind? Marcus said yes. Now Priya can answer him. That is *clarifying*: asking so that something fuzzy becomes clear.

Good clarifying questions are short and honest. Can you say that again? What do you mean by fair? Are you saying the ending was good, or that it made sense? Can you give an example? None of these are dumb. Every one of them helps the whole circle, because if you were lost, someone else was too.

Clarifying also works when the speaker is a teacher, a video or a guest. Write down the parts you did not catch. Then ask about them. A listener who asks one good question learns more than a listener who nods at everything. Nodding is not the same as understanding.

words.d: asking a question so that something unclear becomes clear
one specific case that shows what a bigger idea means

look.title: The Nod
look.text: A guest comes to class to talk about her job as a nurse. She says, Most of my day is triage. Half the class nods. Nobody knows what triage means. Elena raises her hand. What does triage mean? The nurse smiles and explains: deciding who needs help first. Now the whole class understands the rest of her talk.
look.prompt: Why did so many students nod at a word they did not know? What did Elena's question do for everyone else in the room?

check.q: What is a clarifying question?
choices: A question that asks so an unclear idea becomes clear
A question that proves the speaker wrong
A question you already know the answer to
check.why: Clarifying means making something clear. You ask because you are not sure yet.

check.q: Why is nodding not the same as understanding?
choices: You can nod and still be lost
check.why: Half the class nodded at triage without knowing the word. A nod can hide confusion.

check.q: Which is a good clarifying question?
choices: Is this going to be on the test?
Do we have to listen to this?
check.why: Asking for an example is a short, honest way to make a fuzzy idea clear.

lessons.title: Put It in Order
lessons.mainIdea: A short talk needs a clear order: tell what it is about, give two or three parts in a sequence, and end on purpose.
reading: Elena has to give a two-minute talk about her grandmother's tamales. Her first try jumps around: the steaming, then the corn husks, then back to the filling, then her cousin's birthday. Her class is lost. Her second try goes in *order*: first, the filling. Second, the wrapping. Third, the steaming. Now they can follow.

A short talk has three parts. The opening tells the audience what the talk is about in one or two sentences. The middle gives two or three main points, one at a time, in an order that makes sense. The ending says the big idea one more time, or tells why it matters. Do not just stop. End.

Words that show the order help a listener stay with you. First, next, then, finally. Another reason is. The last thing is. These are signposts. A reader can look back at a page. A listener cannot rewind you. Signposts tell them where they are and what is coming.

words.d: the sequence a talk follows so a listener can follow it: first, next, last
a word like first, next or finally that tells a listener where you are in the talk

look.title: Elena's Second Try
look.text: My grandmother makes tamales every December, and it takes all day. First, she cooks the filling in a big pot. Next, she spreads dough on corn husks and adds the filling. Then she rolls and ties each one. Finally, she steams them for an hour. When you smell them, you know it is almost Christmas.
look.prompt: Find the opening, the middle steps and the ending. Circle the signpost words. What would be lost if the steps were mixed up?

check.q: What are the three parts of a short talk?
choices: A joke, a story, a joke
An opening, a middle with main points, an ending
A question, an answer, a question
A list, a picture, a bow
check.why: The opening says what the talk is about, the middle gives the points in order, the ending closes on purpose.

check.q: Why are signpost words extra important in a talk?
choices: A listener cannot rewind you the way a reader can look back
check.why: Words like first and finally tell a listener where they are, since they cannot reread what you said.

check.q: What was wrong with Elena's first try?
choices: The parts were out of order
check.why: She jumped from steaming to husks to filling. The class could not follow the sequence.

lessons.title: Details That Help
lessons.mainIdea: A talk comes alive with a few specific details, facts and examples that support each main point.
reading: Marcus gives a talk about Lake Michigan. First try: Lake Michigan is really big and cool. That is a claim with nothing under it. Second try: Lake Michigan is so big that from a Chicago beach you cannot see the other side. It touches four states. Now the audience has something to picture. Those are *details*.

A detail is a specific fact, example or description that supports a main point. Big is not a detail. Cannot see the other side is. Each main point in your talk needs at least one detail under it. Pick the one that a listener could repeat to a friend later. That is the one that will stick.

Do not pile on. Three strong details beat ten weak ones. If a fact does not support your point, leave it out, even if you like it. And if you say a number or a name, be sure of it. A talk with one wrong fact makes the audience doubt the rest.

words.d: a specific fact, example or description that supports a main point
a statement you want the audience to believe

look.title: Details Under Each Point
look.prompt: Marcus went from zero details to two and the class could picture the lake. Jamal used nine and the class got lost. What does that tell you about how many to use?

check.q: Which one is a detail?
choices: From a Chicago beach you cannot see the other side.
check.why: It is a specific fact that a listener can picture. 'Big' and 'cool' are not specific.

check.q: How many details should each main point have?
check.why: Each point needs at least one detail under it. Three strong ones beat ten weak ones.

check.q: Why does one wrong fact hurt a whole talk?
choices: It makes the talk too long
It makes the audience doubt the rest
check.why: If the audience catches one mistake, they start to wonder what else is wrong.

lessons.title: Pace and Volume
lessons.mainIdea: Speak slowly enough to be understood, loudly enough to reach the back, and pause where a period would go.
reading: Priya knows her talk cold. She gets up and races through it in forty seconds. The class hears a blur. She sat down thinking she did fine. The words were right. The *pace*, the speed of her talking, was wrong. Nervous speakers almost always go too fast, because fast feels like it will be over sooner.

Slow down more than feels normal. What feels slow to you sounds normal to a listener. Pause at the end of each sentence, right where a period would go. Breathe there. A pause is not empty time. It is the moment your listener catches up.

Then think about *volume*, how loud you are. Do not yell. Aim your voice at the person in the back row and speak so they can hear every word. Lift your chin. Your voice goes where your face points. If your face points at the floor, your words go there too.

words.d: how fast or slow you speak
how loud or soft you speak

look.title: The Same Sentence, Three Ways
look.text: Try this out loud. Say: My grandmother makes tamales every December. Say it as fast as you can, all in one rush. Now say it at a normal talking pace. Now say it slowly, with a tiny pause after grandmother and after tamales, looking at the far wall. Notice which one you would want to hear if you were sitting in the back.
look.prompt: Which version was easiest to understand? Why do nervous speakers pick the fast one anyway?

check.q: What does pace mean?
choices: How fast or slow you speak
check.why: Pace is speed. Priya's words were right, but her pace was too fast.

check.q: Where is a good place to pause in a talk?
choices: In the middle of a word
At the end of each sentence
check.why: Pause where a period would go. That is when the listener catches up.

check.q: Why does lifting your chin help your volume?
choices: Your voice goes where your face points
The teacher can see your eyes
check.why: If your face points at the floor, your words go to the floor. Aim at the back row.

lessons.title: Pictures and Objects
lessons.mainIdea: A picture or object can show what words alone cannot, but it should help the point, not replace it.
reading: Elena brings a corn husk to her tamale talk. She holds it up when she says, she spreads dough on corn husks. Suddenly the class understands what a husk is. Nobody needed a definition. That is a *visual aid*: something the audience can see that helps them understand.

A visual aid can be a real object, a photo, a drawing, a map or a simple *chart*. Marcus showed a map of Lake Michigan touching four states. Jamal drew a dinosaur next to a school bus. It showed the size. Each one did a job that words could not do as well.

Two rules. First, the visual should help the point, not decorate it. If you cannot say what it shows, leave it out. Second, do not hide behind it. Hold it up, let people look, say what it shows, then put it down and keep talking to the audience. The aid is a helper. You are still the talk.

words.d: an object, picture, map or chart the audience can see that helps them understand a point
a simple picture that shows numbers or facts so they are easy to compare

look.title: Which One Helps?
look.text: Jamal is choosing a visual for his dinosaur talk. Option one: a drawing of a Tyrannosaurus next to a school bus, showing they are about the same length. Option two: a cool dinosaur sticker with flames on it. Option three: a photo of himself at the museum with his thumb up. His main point is that some dinosaurs were as long as a bus.
look.prompt: Which visual actually helps the main point? What do the other two do instead?

check.q: What is a visual aid?
choices: Something the audience can see that helps a point
A note card you read from
check.why: A husk, a map or a drawing is something the audience sees that helps them understand.

check.q: Why did Elena's corn husk work so well?
choices: It showed what words alone could not show as fast
check.why: Seeing the husk explained the word in one second. That is what a good visual does.

check.q: What should you do after holding up a visual?
choices: Keep it in front of your face
Pass it around and stop talking
Put it away before anyone sees it
Say what it shows, then keep talking to the audience
check.why: The aid is a helper. Show it, explain it, then come back to your audience.

lessons.title: Record and Listen Back
lessons.mainIdea: Recording yourself and listening back shows you what your audience hears, so you can fix it before it counts.
reading: Priya records her talk on a tablet and plays it back. She is shocked. She says um eleven times. She rushes the ending. She says like every few seconds. None of that felt real while she was talking. Now she can hear it. A *recording* shows you what your audience hears, not what you meant.

Listen back for four things. Pace: are you racing? Volume: can you hear every word? Fillers: um, like, you know, so. And the ending: did you end on purpose or just stop? Write down one thing to fix. Just one. Record again. Then pick the next thing.

It feels strange to hear your own voice. Everybody hates it the first time. That feeling passes, and what is left is the fastest way to get better at speaking that there is. Athletes watch film. Singers listen to takes. Speakers listen back.

words.d: a saved copy of your voice or video that you can play back
a sound or word like um or like that fills space while you think

look.title: Priya's Fillers, Three Takes
look.unit: ums and likes in a two-minute talk
look.prompt: Priya fixed only one thing between takes. What do the numbers suggest about the value of listening back?

check.q: Why record yourself giving a talk?
choices: To hear what your audience hears
check.why: A recording shows you what the audience hears, not what you meant to sound like.

check.q: What is a filler?
choices: A detail that supports a point
A sound like um that fills space while you think
check.why: Um, like and you know are fillers. They take up space without saying anything.

check.q: How many things should you fix between recordings?
check.why: Pick one thing, fix it, record again. Priya's ums dropped from eleven to two that way.

lessons.title: Audience and Purpose
lessons.mainIdea: Who is listening and why you are talking should change your words, your details and your tone.
reading: Elena gives her tamale talk twice. Once to her class. Once to a room of kindergartners. To her class she says, the dough is made from corn that has been soaked and ground. To the little kids she says, the dough is soft and yellow, like play dough you can eat. Same talk. Different *audience*. Different words.

The audience is who is listening. Before you speak, ask: What do they already know? What do they care about? Kindergartners do not know what ground corn is. Your class does. A room of parents wants something different again. Change your words and details to fit the people in front of you.

The *purpose* is why you are talking. To teach how tamales are made? To make people laugh? To convince the principal to have a tamale day? Each purpose changes what you say first and what you leave out. A speaker who knows the audience and the purpose has already won half the room.

words.d: the people who are listening to you
the reason you are speaking: to teach, to entertain or to convince

look.title: One Topic, Three Rooms
look.text: Marcus has to talk about Lake Michigan three times. First, to first graders during buddy reading. Second, to his own class for a science grade. Third, to the school board, asking for a field trip to the lakefront. Same lake. Three rooms. In one room he needs simple words. In one he needs facts. In one he needs a reason they should say yes.
look.prompt: Match each room to what it needs. What one fact about the lake would you use for each audience?

check.q: What is an audience?
check.why: The audience is who is listening. Their age and knowledge change your words.

check.q: Why did Elena change 'ground corn' to 'like play dough you can eat'?
choices: Her audience was kindergartners who did not know ground corn
check.why: Kindergartners do not know what ground corn is. She picked words they could picture.

check.q: Which is a purpose for a talk?
choices: To convince the principal to have a tamale day
check.why: Purpose is the reason you speak. Convincing the principal is a reason.

review.q: What made the book club's second try better than the first?
choices: People listened, said back and asked questions
Ms. Nakamura told them the answer
They stopped talking about the book
review.why: Nobody changed their vote, but each person could explain the other side. Listening did that.

review.q: What is the best way to prepare for a book discussion?
choices: Read it all, mark spots and bring one question
Wait and see what others say
review.why: Preparing means reading the whole text, marking places and bringing something to say.

choices: I see it differently because the text says she chose.
I disagree and I will not say why.
review.why: It disagrees with the idea and gives a reason from the text without attacking anyone.

review.q: A speaker talks for one minute. What should your summary keep?
choices: Their main point and biggest reasons
review.why: A summary is short, in your words, and keeps the point and the reasons.

review.q: Which words are signposts in a talk?
review.why: First, next and finally tell a listener where they are in the order of the talk.

review.q: Nervous speakers usually talk too fast. What should they do?
choices: Slow down and pause at the end of sentences
review.why: Slow feels strange to the speaker but normal to the listener. Pauses let people catch up.

review.q: Which visual aid best supports the point that some dinosaurs were as long as a bus?
choices: A drawing of a dinosaur next to a school bus
review.why: The drawing shows the size comparison. The others decorate but do not help the point.

review.q: Why would Elena describe tamale dough differently to kindergartners than to her class?
choices: Kindergartners are not a real audience
A different audience knows different things
review.why: Audience changes your words. Little kids do not know what ground corn is, so she used play dough.
